traveler: Nabucodonosor II (Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon)
title: The Chronicle and the Brick: from the House of Ishtar at Uruk to the Burning of the Temple
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Uruk, Eanna: the house of Ishtar
stops.date_confidence: no birth record survives for any king of this dynasty; c. 642 BC is a modern back-calculation, and the Eanna office is a reconstruction repeated by encyclopedias rather than a datum from any dated inscription
stops.campa: Nabopolassar has broken Assyria and made himself king in Babylon, and his eldest son is sent south to Uruk, to Eanna, the precinct of Ishtar, older than any dynasty that has ever governed it. Tradition puts the boy's birth in this city and an office in this temple before his father names him crown prince and general. No Babylonian tablet records the birth of a king of this house, and none records the appointment. Both details reach us from encyclopedias repeating one another, and the chronicles are silent until he is a grown man at the head of an army.
suggested_refs: The Eanna precinct at Uruk, whose building texts of this period are of disputed attribution

stops.name: Harran, the last Assyrian city
stops.date_confidence: the capture of Harran is attested to years 16 and 17 of Nabopolassar; Nebuchadnezzar's presence is not. ABC 3 names only the king of Akkad here, and the chronicle series first names Nebuchadnezzar in the 607 BC entry
stops.campa: Assyria dies by pieces. Nineveh fell four years ago and what is left of the empire has drawn back to Harran under Ashur-uballit, propped up by Egyptian troops. The Babylonian army takes the city, and the chronicle names one man in the taking, the king of Akkad, his father. No crown prince appears in the tablet. Modern accounts put Nebuchadnezzar in the line of battle here because it is where a general's apprenticeship ought to be, and the text says nothing either way.
suggested_refs: ABC 3, the Fall of Nineveh Chronicle, years 16-17 of Nabopolassar
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, translation on livius.org

stops.name: Bit-Hanunia in Urartu, the march into the mountains
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month Elul of the nineteenth year of Nabopolassar; the site of Bit-Hanunia is unidentified and the pin is an approximate point where the upper Tigris enters the highlands
stops.campa: In the month Elul he follows the bank of the Tigris north, up past the plain and into the mountains of Bit-Hanunia in the district of Urartu, and stays there some months. This is the first entry in the whole chronicle series that names him. He is a field commander in high country, taking hostages and cattle from places no scribe in Babylon needs to find on a map. Where Bit-Hanunia stood is still not known, and the tablet gives no other bearing than the river.
suggested_refs: The Wiseman Chronicle entry for the nineteenth year of Nabopolassar
sources: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 3 / Wiseman, Chronicles of Chaldaean Kings)

stops.name: Carchemish, the crossing of the Euphrates
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the chronicle and cross-dated by Jeremiah 46:2 to the fourth year of Jehoiakim; the chronicle gives no month, and the spring placing is a campaigning-season estimate
stops.campa: At the ford where the Euphrates bends into Syria, Necho II holds the crossing with the last Assyrian field army beside him. Nebuchadnezzar crosses and destroys them both, and the Egyptian empire in Asia ends at that ford. Five hundred miles south, in Judah, a prophet dates the fourth year of Jehoiakim by this battle, which means the news travels fast and lands hard. He is not yet king. He commands for his father, and the army obeys him as though he were.
suggested_refs: The Carchemish battlefield at Jerablus, excavated by Woolley and Lawrence before the First World War

stops.name: Hamath, the pursuit down the Orontes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the campaign season; the chronicle gives no month
stops.campa: He does not let the beaten army reform. The pursuit runs south down the Orontes and catches Necho's remnant in the district of Hamath, where it is finished in open country, with the river on one side and nothing behind it to fall back on. All Hatti-land now pays to Babylon, and the Syrian cities bring their tribute in to a crown prince who has no throne of his own. The chronicle sets the whole season down in the flat administrative voice it keeps for grain deliveries and temple repairs.
stops.quote: not a single man escaped to his own country
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5), on the destruction of the Egyptian remnant at Hamath
suggested_refs: ABC 5, the campaign notice for the twenty-first year of Nabopolassar

stops.name: Babylon, the Southern Palace: he sits on the throne
stops.date_confidence: attested. ABC 5 puts Nabopolassar's death on 8 Abu, 15 August 605 BC, and has Nebuchadnezzar sit on the royal throne on 1 Ululu, 7 September 605 BC. Readings that treat 15 August as a separate accession act of his own conflate the father's death with the son's enthronement; the earlier atlas file on this king takes that reading and this file does not
stops.campa: On the eighth of Abu, Nabopolassar dies in Babylon. His son is in Syria with the army and the tribute of a whole conquered province. Berossus, three centuries later, has him cross the desert with a light escort while the column follows behind. On the first of Ululu he sits on the royal throne in Babylon: twenty-three days from a father's death to a son's enthronement, with no rival named in any list that survives. Before the year ends he is back in Hatti-land and the tribute comes to him there.
suggested_refs: The Southern Palace mound at Babylon, seat of the court for the whole reign

stops.name: Ashkelon, the city made a ruin heap
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month Kislev of the accession year
stops.campa: In the month Kislev of his accession year he turns into Philistia. Ashkelon has refused submission and is taken, plundered, and turned into a ruin heap, and its king is carried away. The excavators find him out twenty-five centuries later in a burn layer with smashed storage jars in it and a winery destroyed with the vintage still inside. He marches home in the month Shebat with the spoil, and the harbour lies empty behind him; the site is not properly resettled for generations.
suggested_refs: The 604 BC destruction layer at Tel Ashkelon, excavated by the Leon Levy Expedition

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: Jehoiakim becomes his servant
stops.date_confidence: traditional. 2 Kings 24:1 gives no year, and no Babylonian text names Jerusalem in this window; 604 or 603 BC is inferred from the fall of Ashkelon
stops.campa: Ashkelon is four days' march from Jerusalem and the lesson does not need repeating. Jehoiakim, whom Egypt put on this throne, becomes the servant of the king of Babylon and pays for three years. Judah is tributary to a man who has held his own throne barely a year. There is no siege in the account, no army at the wall, and no Babylonian tablet that names Jerusalem in these years at all. The submission is dated by inference from the ash at Ashkelon.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 24:1, the three years of Jehoiakim's vassalage

stops.name: The Egyptian frontier, the battle both armies lose
stops.date_confidence: attested to the fourth regnal year, winter 601/600 BC; the battle site is not named in the chronicle and the Pelusium pin is a reconstruction
stops.campa: In the fourth year he marches on Egypt itself. The two armies meet on the frontier and maul each other, and the chronicle, which exists to record the king's victories, sets down that heavy losses fell on both sides and that the king of Akkad turned back to Babylon. He spends the whole of the next year at home in Babylon, replacing horses, chariots, and men. Judah is watching from between the two powers, and draws the conclusion Egypt wants it to draw.
suggested_refs: ABC 5, the fourth regnal year, the one entry admitting Babylonian losses

stops.name: The Kedarite steppe, the raid on the Arabs
stops.date_confidence: attested to the sixth regnal year; the place is not attested at all, and the Dumat al-Jandal pin is reconstructed from Jeremiah 49:28-33
stops.campa: With Egypt held off, he takes the army into the desert against the Arabs of Kedar, striking tent camps and wells instead of towns and walls. The chronicle counts only what is carried off: flocks, herds, gods, and people. No place-name survives in the cuneiform for this campaign, and the location shown here is reconstructed out of Jeremiah, who never saw the steppe and writes the raid as a sentence pronounced on a nation that dwells alone, without gates and without bars.
suggested_refs: Jeremiah 49:28-33, the oracle against Kedar and Hazor

stops.name: Jerusalem, the City of David: the second day of Adar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: 2 Adar of the seventh year, converted to 15 or 16 March 597 BC depending on the reckoning used
stops.campa: Jehoiakim is dead and his eighteen-year-old son has reigned three months. The king of Akkad musters his troops, marches to Hatti-land, and sits down before the city, and on the second day of Adar it opens to him. He appoints a king of his own choosing there, takes the heavy tribute out of the city, and sends it back to Babylon. This is the one dated day on which the Babylonian record and the Hebrew record touch and agree, down to the month and the number of the day.
stops.quote: the king of Akkad mustered his troops, marched to the Hatti-land, and besieged the city of Judah and on the second day of the month of Addaru he seized the city and captured the king
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 (BM 21946, the Jerusalem Chronicle), livius.org translation. Grayson's 1975 rendering differs in wording and is not blended in here
suggested_refs: BM 21946, the Jerusalem Chronicle, in the British Museum

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: the first stripping
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the deportation follows the capture by weeks and no day is given for it
stops.campa: He takes the treasures of the house of the Lord and cuts up the gold vessels Solomon made, and carries out the king, his mother, his wives, his officers, the craftsmen and the smiths, ten thousand of them in the count that survives. Among them goes a priest named Ezekiel, who will date his visions from the years of this captivity and prophesy against the man who ordered it, by name. Mattaniah, uncle of the deposed boy, is left on the throne and renamed Zedekiah.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 24:10-17 and Ezekiel 1:1-2, the same deportation counted from both ends

stops.name: Susa, the march that turns back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the ninth regnal year; Susa as the objective is a reconstruction, since the surviving text names no destination
stops.campa: In the ninth year he moves east out of Babylon, along the Tigris, toward Elam. There is no battle. The Elamite king hears that he is coming, and fear falls on him, and he goes back to his own country; the Babylonian army stands where it stands a while and then goes home. Whether Susa was the objective the tablet never says, and the surviving text names no destination for the march at all. Elam is not subdued and not garrisoned, and the chronicle does not mention it again.
suggested_refs: ABC 5, ninth regnal year, the Elamite withdrawal

stops.name: Babylon, the revolt in the land
stops.date_confidence: attested to the tenth regnal year, with the king recorded at home in Babylon from Kislev to Tebet
stops.campa: In the tenth year there is rebellion inside Babylonia. The chronicle is brief and terrible about it: he takes the ringleaders, and with his own arms he slays many of his own army. Who they were, what they wanted, whether any of it reached the palace stair, the tablet does not say. It is the only rising inside Babylonia that the surviving record mentions in forty-three years. He is in Babylon from Kislev to Tebet that winter, which is not where a king of Akkad usually spends a campaigning season.
stops.quote: put his numerous army to the sword
suggested_refs: ABC 5, tenth regnal year, the domestic revolt of 595 BC

stops.name: Riblah on the Orontes, where the record stops
stops.date_confidence: attested to the eleventh regnal year, the last entry before ABC 5 breaks off. Riblah as the base is inference; the chronicle says only Hatti-land
stops.campa: Riblah is a camp on the Orontes halfway between Babylon and the sea, and for two decades the west is governed from it. Tribute arrives here, and captured kings are brought here for judgment. In the eleventh year he musters and marches to Hatti-land again, and there the tablet breaks off in mid-entry. What is known of the years after it comes from Judah, from Josephus quoting Greek books that no longer exist, and from undated brick. Thirty-two years of the reign have no chronicle at all.
suggested_refs: The break in ABC 5 after the eleventh regnal year, 594 BC

stops.name: Babylon, the storerooms: rations for Yaukin
stops.date_confidence: the ration tablets are dated by regnal year to around 592 BC; individual tablets in the group run across several years
stops.campa: Under the palace, in vaulted rooms beside the gate, the ration lists are kept. Koldewey's men dig them out at the start of the twentieth century, and nobody reads the names in them for another twenty years. Among the oil and barley issued to hostages, craftsmen and foreign specialists there stands an allowance for Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud, and for his five sons. He has been in Babylon five years by then. He is still given his title in the ledger, and he is not released.
suggested_refs: The Weidner ration tablets from the vaulted storerooms at Babylon
sources: Weidner ration tablets, excavated by Koldewey's expedition

segments.name: The Second Siege and the Burning

stops.name: Jerusalem, the walls: the tenth day of the tenth month
stops.date_confidence: 10 Tevet of Zedekiah's ninth year, mid-January 588 BC by the usual reckoning. Flagged: this file also carries the burning in 586 BC, which makes the siege about thirty months rather than the eighteen the sources describe. The 587 and 586 chronologies cannot both stand, no chronicle tablet survives for these years, and the contradiction is left visible rather than smoothed
stops.campa: Zedekiah, who has reigned nine years on a throne Babylon gave him, stops the tribute and looks to Egypt. On the tenth day of the tenth month the army comes up and builds forts against the city round about, a bank of earth and timber thrown up against a wall of stone. A relieving force from Egypt comes and goes and changes nothing. Inside the wall the bread runs out, and the prophet Jeremiah, held in the court of the guard, tells whoever will hear him to go out and surrender.
stops.quote: And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4, the opening of the eighteen-month siege

stops.name: Lachish, the fires that go out
stops.date_confidence: the destruction layer is dated to the campaign of 588-587 BC; no source gives a day, and the letters themselves are undated
stops.campa: Lachish is the strongest place in Judah after Jerusalem, a double wall on a mound above the Shephelah, and it is reduced first. In the last weeks an officer writes in to the commander that they are watching for the signal fires of Lachish according to all the signs, because they can no longer see Azekah. Azekah has already gone dark. The sherd is found where it was dropped, in the burnt gate chamber, in a metre of ash with the arrowheads and the sling stones lying in it.
suggested_refs: Lachish Letter IV, found in the burnt gate chamber of level II
sources: Lachish excavation, destruction layer II (Starkey, Ussishkin)

stops.name: The plains of Jericho, Zedekiah overtaken
stops.date_confidence: attested in sequence, days before the burning; no date is given in either account
stops.campa: The wall is breached at night and the king goes out with his men of war by the gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, running for the Jordan. The Chaldean column overtakes him in the plains of Jericho, open ground a thousand feet below the level of the sea, with no cover in any direction, and his army scatters from around him. He is taken alive, on the road down to the river. From the breach in the wall to the place where they catch him is under twenty miles.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 25:4-5 and Jeremiah 39:4-5, the flight by the king's garden

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: the burning
stops.date_confidence: 7 to 10 Av of the nineteenth regnal year, late July or August. Whether the year is 587 or 586 is disputed and unresolved by any surviving chronicle tablet; the date here is arithmetically inconsistent with the siege stop, and that inconsistency belongs to the sources, not to a choice made here
stops.campa: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, comes up from Riblah in the fifth month and burns the house of the Lord, the king's house, and every great house in the city. Nebuchadnezzar is not at the breach; he is at the camp on the Orontes, and the fire is set by an officer acting on his order. The platform stays bare for the length of a lifetime. The bronze pillars Solomon set up, the sea and the bases under it, are broken small, weighed out, and carried to Babylon as metal. The walls are pulled down all round.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 25:8-17 and Jeremiah 52:12-23, the inventory of what was broken up and weighed

stops.name: Riblah, the judgment on Zedekiah
stops.date_confidence: attested in sequence rather than by date; the account gives no day
stops.campa: Zedekiah is brought north up the Orontes to the camp at Riblah and stood in front of the king he swore to. They kill his sons in front of him, and the nobles of Judah with them. Then they put out his eyes, bind him in two bronze fetters, and send him to Babylon. The order of the two acts is the sentence: the killing is arranged to be the last thing he sees. He has reigned eleven years, all of them at Babylon's pleasure. He dies in prison in Babylon, and neither Kings nor Jeremiah says when.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 25:6-7 and Jeremiah 39:6-7, the sentence given at Riblah

stops.name: Mizpah in Benjamin, Gedaliah made governor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the months after the burning; no date is given. Gedaliah's murder follows in the seventh month of an unstated year
stops.campa: He puts no son of David on any throne. He appoints Gedaliah, a Judean official whose family served the old court, as governor over the poorest of the land, the vinedressers and the husbandmen left behind, and seats him not in the burned city but at Mizpah, eight miles north of it. To Mizpah is also sent the prophet Jeremiah, taken out of the chain gang at Ramah under a specific instruction about his handling issued in the king's own name. Within months Gedaliah is murdered at his own table.
stops.quote: Now Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon gave charge concerning Jeremiah to Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, saying, Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm; but do unto him even as he shall say unto thee.
suggested_refs: Tell en-Nasbeh, identified with Mizpah of Benjamin, seat of the Babylonian governor

stops.name: Tahpanhes, the stones at Pharaoh's door
stops.date_confidence: the flight to Egypt follows Gedaliah's murder, which is undated by year; whether the throne was ever set on those stones is unattested on the Babylonian and the Egyptian side alike
stops.campa: The survivors of Gedaliah's murder run for Egypt and take Jeremiah with them against his will. At Tahpanhes, in the frontier town where Judean refugees have settled, he takes great stones and hides them in the clay of the brick pavement at the entry of Pharaoh's house, in front of witnesses, and says that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne upon these stones and spread his royal pavilion over them. No Babylonian and no Egyptian source says that he ever did.
suggested_refs: Jeremiah 43:8-13, the buried stones at the entry of Pharaoh's house

segments.name: The Island, the Cedar, and the Nile

stops.name: Tyre, the siege of the island begins
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Menander of Ephesus, quoted by Josephus, gives thirteen years in the reign of Ithobaal III; the start is placed at 586 or 585 BC by working backwards from the end
stops.campa: Tyre stands half a mile offshore behind a wall that comes down to the water, with two harbours and a fleet, and the army that burned Jerusalem cannot swim. He invests it anyway. The Tyrian records, which Menander of Ephesus read and Josephus copied out of him, count thirteen years of it, in the reign of Ithobaal. Every head in that army is rubbed bare and every shoulder worn raw, Ezekiel writes afterwards, from hauling siege works up against a city they cannot enter.
suggested_refs: Josephus, Against Apion 1.21, preserving Menander of Ephesus on the thirteen years
sources: Josephus, Against Apion 1.21, citing Menander of Ephesus

stops.name: Rabbath-Ammon, the campaign beyond the Jordan
stops.date_confidence: the deportation is attested to the twenty-third regnal year by Jeremiah 52:30; Josephus alone dates the Transjordan campaign, and no cuneiform source mentions it
stops.campa: In the twenty-third year the army goes over the Jordan against the Ammonites and the Moabites and subdues them both. Ammon had sheltered the men who murdered his governor at Mizpah four years earlier. In the same year seven hundred and forty-five more Judeans are carried away to Babylon, the third and smallest of the deportations the book of Jeremiah counts, and the last one it counts. The only witness to the Transjordan campaign is Josephus, writing six centuries later, and there is no cuneiform trace of it at all.
suggested_refs: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 10.181-182; Jeremiah 52:30, the third deportation

stops.name: Wadi Brisa, the cedar road
stops.date_confidence: undated within the reign, 604 to 562 BC. The year shown is a placeholder in the middle of the reign and carries no evidential weight
stops.campa: High on a pass between the Bekaa and the coast, on the road the cedar comes down, he has two reliefs cut into the rock face and a long inscription set beside each. In one panel he stands before a felled cedar. In the other he fights a lion. The text is about logistics and it is proud of them: a road driven through country the inscription calls impassable, so that the cedars of Lebanon can be dragged whole to Babylon for the roof of Marduk's house.
stops.quote: On that day, Lebanon, the mountain of cedars, the luxuriant forest of Marduk, of sweet smell, whose excellent cedars...
stops.quote_source: Wadi Brisa rock inscription, in the wording widely reproduced from secondary sources. Flagged unverified: it could not be checked against Da Riva's critical edition of 2012, which was not reachable
suggested_refs: The twin rock reliefs at Wadi esh-Sharbin, edited by Rocio Da Riva (2012)
sources: Da Riva, The Twin Inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar at Brisa (2012)

stops.name: Nahr el-Kalb, the ledger of conquerors
stops.date_confidence: undated within the reign; no year can be recovered from the stele, whose text is largely gone
stops.campa: Where the Dog River comes out of the mountains the coast road squeezes past a cliff, and every army that has used the road has cut its name into the rock. Ramesses is here. Esarhaddon is here. He puts his own stele among them, in cuneiform, facing the sea. The stone is soft and the sea air has eaten it, so that his name and titles can be made out and the rest cannot. The empires that come after cut theirs in Greek, in Latin, in Arabic, and in French.
suggested_refs: The Nahr el-Kalb inscription series, documented by the Factum Foundation
sources: Factum Foundation documentation, Nahr el-Kalb inscriptions

stops.name: Tyre, the submission without a conquest
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from Menander's thirteen years; no Babylonian record of the outcome exists, and some historians dispute the whole reconstruction on that ground
stops.campa: Thirteen years end and the island is still an island. Tyre submits on terms, keeps its own king under Babylonian suzerainty, and pays. The army is not let into the streets and there is no plunder to divide. Ezekiel, who had prophesied the city's fall, writes the outcome down against himself: the king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyre, and yet had he no wages, nor his army. Not one Babylonian inscription mentions Tyre at all.
suggested_refs: Ezekiel 29:18, conceding that the Tyre campaign yielded nothing

stops.name: The Egyptian frontier, the thirty-seventh year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the thirty-seventh regnal year by BM 33041, which names Amasis and then breaks off; the location is a reconstruction, since the tablet gives none
stops.campa: A single tablet in London, broken across the middle and legible only in part, records a campaign against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year and names Amasis, king of Egypt. Then it breaks. It gives no place, no outcome, and no second witness anywhere in cuneiform. Forty years after Carchemish, this fragment is the last military notice of the reign. Whether the army crossed into the Delta, what happened when it did, and how the thing ended are all in the half that is missing.
suggested_refs: BM 33041, the fragmentary chronicle tablet naming Amasis

stops.name: Sippar, the temple of the sun
stops.date_confidence: undated. The c. 599 BC in circulation is subtracted from Nabonidus's remark that the wall sagged after forty-five years, and is not read from any text of Nebuchadnezzar's own
stops.campa: At Sippar on the Euphrates the sun god judges, and his temple, Ebabbar, is old before Babylon is anything at all. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilds it, and no inscription of his own puts a year on the work. The date in circulation is arithmetic done on a complaint made by a later king. Nabonidus, digging for the original foundations two reigns on, records that a former king built this wall and that after forty-five years the wall sagged, so that he had to take it down and start again.
suggested_refs: The Sippar Cylinder of Nabonidus, recording the forty-five-year interval

stops.name: Opis, the wall between the rivers
stops.date_confidence: undated, and the attribution itself is reconstruction: Xenophon writes some two hundred years later and names no builder, and no Babylonian text places Nebuchadnezzar on this line of works
stops.campa: Where the Tigris and the Euphrates come nearest to each other, north of Babylon, a wall and a system of canals runs across the gap against whatever comes down out of the north. His father began it and he continues it. Two hundred years afterwards Xenophon marches past the thing with ten thousand Greeks, measures it, calls it the Median Wall, and does not say who built it. No Babylonian text names him on this line either, so the attribution rests on a Greek who was only passing.
suggested_refs: Xenophon, Anabasis 2.4.12, on the wall the Greeks called Median

stops.name: Babylon, Esagila: the house of Marduk
stops.date_confidence: undated. The building inscriptions describe the work at length and carry no regnal year; the year shown is a placeholder, and the c. 590 BC found in some compilations has nothing behind it
stops.campa: Esagila is the house of Marduk and the reason Babylon is Babylon. He rebuilds and enlarges it, sheathes the inner chamber in gold, and says so in the first person at length, on cylinders buried inside the walls for no reader but the god and whichever king digs there next. Not one of these texts carries a date, and none of them says when the work began or when it stopped. Forty-three years of building come down to us without a single regnal year attached to any of it.
stops.quote: he adorned the temple of Bel, and the other temples, after an elegant manner, out of the spoils he had taken in this war
stops.quote_source: Berossus, Babyloniaca III, quoted in Josephus, Against Apion 1.19, Whiston translation
suggested_refs: The East India House Inscription and the Esagila building cylinders
sources: Nebuchadnezzar building inscriptions (East India House Inscription and others)

stops.name: Babylon, Etemenanki: to rival heaven
stops.date_confidence: undated within the reign; the c. 580 BC in circulation has no source behind it and is not carried as evidence here
stops.campa: The stepped tower stands in its own walled court beside the temple, stages of mud brick with a shrine on top, and he raises its head, in his own phrase, to rival heaven. Later readers give the tower another name out of Genesis, and the confusion of tongues fastens itself to a building rebuilt to be legible. Koldewey finds the foundation and almost nothing else: the brick was quarried away by the villages for two thousand years. Herodotus, a century after, describes the ascent stage by stage, and the spiral way round the outside of it.
stops.quote_source: Nebuchadnezzar's building inscriptions on Etemenanki (East India House Inscription; George, House Most High)
suggested_refs: The excavated foundation of Etemenanki, cleared by Koldewey
sources: Andrew George, 'The Tower of Babel', AfO 51 (2005)

stops.name: Borsippa, the house of Nabu
stops.date_confidence: undated within the reign; the Borsippa cylinder records the work without a regnal year
stops.campa: Eleven miles south-west across the marsh, Nabu the god of writing keeps his house, and once a year the son goes up the road to visit the father at Babylon while the whole country walks behind him. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilds Ezida and its tower and buries cylinders in the brickwork asking for a long life, a stable throne, and old age. The prayer is standard; every king of this house buries one. He gets the forty-three years. The ruin is called Birs Nimrud now, and its upper courses are fused to green glass.
suggested_refs: The Borsippa cylinder of Nebuchadnezzar II, recording the rebuilding of Ezida
sources: Borsippa cylinder inscription of Nebuchadnezzar II

stops.name: Babylon, the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way
stops.date_confidence: the principal construction phase is placed around 575 BC on archaeological grounds; the dedicatory inscriptions themselves carry no date. The pin is the canonical atlas point for Babylon's gate, which sits some hundreds of metres from the coordinate Wikipedia gives for the excavated gate
stops.campa: The gate is faced in glazed brick the colour of deep water, and on the blue there are bulls and dragons in moulded rows, with lions running the length of the walls of the street beyond. The way is paved in limestone and red breccia, wide enough for the god's carriage at the new year. Every paving block carries his name stamped into it before firing, on the underside as well as the top, so that a man walking to the temple walks on the king's name whether he reads it or not.
suggested_refs: Koldewey's Das wieder erstehende Babylon, on the gate and the processional street
sources: Nebuchadnezzar dedicatory inscriptions found in situ

stops.name: Babylon, the Southern Palace: the king writes himself down
stops.date_confidence: undated. The East India House Inscription was composed at some point between 604 and 562 BC and cannot be placed more closely than that
stops.campa: In the palace at the north end of the inner city he keeps his court, and from it the west is governed by letter. There is not a word about Judah, or Tyre, or Egypt in anything he writes about himself; the building texts record only what was built. What he does say he says in stone, and repeats: prince, favourite of Marduk, beloved of Nabu, arbiter, possessor of wisdom, the untiring governor anxious for the shrines of Babylonia and Borsippa, son of Nabopolassar king of Babylon.
stops.quote: I am Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the exalted prince, the favourite of the god Marduk, the beloved of the god Nabu, the arbiter, the possessor of wisdom, who reverences their lordship, the untiring governor who is constantly anxious for the maintenance of the shrines of Babylonia and Borsippa, the wise, the pious, the son of Nabopolasser, king of Babylon.
stops.quote_source: East India House Inscription, opening titulary, translation as in Records of the Past, 2nd series vol. III
suggested_refs: The East India House Inscription, a limestone foundation tablet in ten columns

stops.name: Babylon, the vaulted terraces
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated. No text of his own reign mentions a garden of any kind; the tradition begins with Berossus, three centuries later, and is repeated by Greek writers later still
stops.campa: Berossus, a priest of Bel writing three hundred years after, says the king raised stone terraces on vaults inside the palace and planted them with trees, to give a wife brought up in Media the sight of a mountain country. No inscription of his own mentions a garden. Josephus, who preserves the passage, gives the wife no name at all; Amytis comes from elsewhere, and her father is Astyages in the text and Cyaxares only by a modern correction. Stephanie Dalley argues the whole wonder belongs to Sennacherib at Nineveh, a century earlier and a different empire.
stops.quote: he rendered the prospect an exact resemblance of a mountainous country. This he did to please his queen, because she had been brought up in Media
stops.quote_source: Berossus, Babyloniaca III, quoted in Josephus, Against Apion 1.19, Whiston translation
suggested_refs: Stephanie Dalley, The Mystery of the Hanging Garden of Babylon (2013)
sources: Dalley, The Mystery of the Hanging Garden of Babylon (2013)

segments.name: The Madness, the Death, and the Digging

stops.name: Babylon, the seven times
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Daniel 4 is composed centuries after the reign and supplies no year; no Babylonian chronicle, ration list, or dated contract records any interruption in the reign
stops.campa: In a book written four centuries later, the king walks on the roof of the palace, says one sentence too many, and is driven out from men to eat grass like an ox until seven times pass over him, his hair grown like eagles' feathers and his nails like birds' claws. Then his reason returns and he blesses the Most High. No Babylonian document of any kind records an interruption in the reign, and the dated contracts run straight through the years the story would have to occupy.
stops.quote: The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
suggested_refs: Daniel 4:28-37, the seven times of the king's madness
sources: absence of corroboration in any Babylonian chronicle or inscription

stops.name: Babylon, the forty-third year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the forty-third regnal year by the administrative date formulas and the Babylonian King List; the month is the usual placing of the transition, and the detail of illness comes from Berossus alone
stops.campa: He dies in Babylon in the forty-third year of the reign, of illness, according to a Babylonian priest writing in Greek long afterwards. No tomb has ever been found; nearly twenty years of German excavation went over the palace and temple precincts and identified nothing as a burial. His son Amel-Marduk takes the throne and in his accession year brings Jehoiachin of Judah out of prison, changes his prison garments, and seats him at the royal table. Jehoiachin has been a prisoner thirty-seven years.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 25:27-30, the release of Jehoiachin in Amel-Marduk's accession year

stops.name: Babylon, the treasury opened
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Nabonidus Chronicle dates the fall of Babylon to 12 October 539 BC. The return of the vessels is dated by Ezra to the first year of Cyrus and the inventory is the biblical one
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after his death the city opens to Cyrus without a battle, and the Persians go through the treasury. The gold and silver vessels cut out of the house in Jerusalem are still there, stored where they were put, and Cyrus has them counted and sent back up the road with the exiles, by the way they came down. Ezra gives the inventory by object and by number: chargers of gold and of silver, knives, bowls, five thousand four hundred vessels in all.
suggested_refs: Ezra 1:7-11, the inventory of returned Temple vessels

stops.name: Qumran, the prayer of the wrong king
stops.date_confidence: the copy is dated on palaeographic grounds to the first century BC; the tradition behind it is older and cannot be dated
stops.campa: In a cave above the Dead Sea a scroll fragment in Aramaic has a king of Babylon afflicted seven years with an evil ulcer at Teima, praying there, and healed by a Jewish exorcist who tells him to give the glory to God. The king in the fragment is Nabonidus, the last of the dynasty, who really did spend years at Teima and really did leave Babylon. Many readers take Daniel's mad Nebuchadnezzar to be this story with the wrong king put into it. The question is open.
suggested_refs: 4Q242, the Prayer of Nabonidus, from Qumran Cave 4
sources: scholarship on the sources of Daniel 4

stops.name: Berlin, the gate rebuilt indoors
stops.date_confidence: attested: the reconstructed gate opened to the public at the Pergamon Museum in 1930, after crates arriving from 1926 and assembly begun in 1928
stops.campa: Koldewey digs Babylon for eighteen years and ships the glazed brick out in crates, hundreds of them, sorted fragment by fragment. The gate is put back together in Berlin out of about half its original facing, the missing pieces made new to match. It opens to the public in 1930 at a fraction of its height, because the room is not tall enough for the rest of it. The processional way runs beside it, indoors, along a museum floor, with the lions at shoulder height.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Ishtar Gate in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin

stops.name: London, the British Museum: his own account
stops.date_confidence: attested: the tablet passed to the British Museum in 1938; the inscription itself was composed at an unknown point between 604 and 562 BC
stops.campa: A limestone tablet cut in an archaic ceremonial script, ten columns of it, stands in a case in Bloomsbury. It came out of Babylon into the collection of the East India Company, hung in their house in Leadenhall Street among the curiosities of a trading firm, and passed to the museum in 1938 when the company's things were dispersed. It is his own account of what he built, in his own voice, and it is the longest thing he left behind. For twenty-three centuries nobody alive could read it.
suggested_refs: The East India House Inscription, British Museum, acquired 1938
sources: World History Encyclopedia, 'The East India House Inscription'

stops.name: Babylon, the bricks of 1987
stops.date_confidence: attested: the reconstruction over the Southern Palace foundations dates to 1987 and 1988, and the stamped-brick text is documented in situ
stops.campa: On top of his walls, on his own foundations, a new palace goes up in the 1980s at the order of a president who has himself photographed in profile beside the king. The bricks are stamped before firing, in the old manner: in the reign of the victorious Saddam Hussein, the rebuilding of the great city of Babylon was done in 1987. Journalism shortens the line to son of Nebuchadnezzar, which is not what the brick says. The method is the old one whatever the wording: the name goes into the course, under the next man's feet. The stamped bricks are still there, in the walls above the excavated foundations.
suggested_refs: The stamped reconstruction bricks of 1987 in the Southern Palace walls at Babylon
sources: World History Encyclopedia, 'Saddam Hussein Plaque in Babylon'
The Archaeologist, 'The Reconstruction of Babylon Under Saddam Hussein'
